cultivar: Various non-Tieguanyin Anxi cultivars (Ben Shan, Mao Xie, Huang Dan, Qi Lan, Mei Zhan, Da Ye Wulong and others), often blended
processing: Anxi-style light oxidation and ball-rolling, finished green or lightly roasted; export grades are usually roasted a little more for shelf stability and blended for consistency.
harvest_season: Spring, summer and autumn of the current year; the category covers every picking, and summer leaf is common in the cheaper grades.
appearance_dry: Mixed green to olive pellets of slightly uneven size and colour, often with a bit more stem than Tieguanyin.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold to light amber depending on the roast, clear.
appearance_wet: A mix of leaf shapes and sizes, oval and serrated, mostly green with reddish edges.
taste_profile: Light florals and honey, sometimes a soft roast, on a modest body with a short, clean finish; pleasant rather than remarkable.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, short steeps in a gaiwan. It also works Western style: 3 g per 200 ml, 2–3 minutes, twice. Roasted export grades are happiest with boiling water.

vintage_note: Sold by the current year, usually without a stated season; export tins are blended lots that may mix pickings and villages, are kept at room temperature when roasted, and are best within a year or two. It is not aged on purpose, and a vintage on the label is rare.
description:
Se Zhong, colour varieties, is not one tea but Anxi's word for everything that is not Tieguanyin: the oolongs made from the county's other cultivars, Ben Shan, Mao Xie, Huang Dan, Qi Lan, Mei Zhan and more, sold singly or, more often, blended. If you have ever bought a tin labelled Fujian oolong or Se Chung without a cultivar name, this is what was in it.

As a formal class it dates from the 1950s, when state commodity inspectors sorted Anxi oolong into Tieguanyin, se zhong and oolong, with the assorted other cultivars in the middle class. The name carried into the export trade, where Se Chung oolong became a standard product in the tins sent to Southeast Asia, Hong Kong and the West. Those export lots are blended for a consistent taste and given a slightly fuller roast so they keep on a shop shelf; domestic se zhong is more likely to be green-style and sold by village.

Processing is Anxi processing: light oxidation, ball-rolling and a light dry or a gentle roast. Because the cultivars differ, the pellets are a bit uneven in size and colour, and the cup is a composite: florals from the Huang Dan and Mao Xie component, a little body from Ben Shan or Mei Zhan, honey and a soft toast from the roast, and a finish that is clean but short.

Brew it short in a gaiwan, or Western style in a pot, with water just off the boil for green lots and boiling for roasted ones; four or five steeps is what it has. It is a decent everyday oolong and a good base to learn from, because it tastes like an average of Anxi.

It is sold by the current year, usually without season, and should be drunk within a year or two. The interesting move is to go the other way: buy the single cultivars, Ben Shan, Mao Xie, Huang Jin Gui, Mei Zhan, under their own names from a seller who states the season, and taste what each one brings to the blend.
sources_note: Se Chung is the older export spelling. The description of the old Anxi grading split (Tieguanyin versus se zhong) follows Chinese trade sources.
history:
Se zhong is a trade class, not a single tea. As a formal grouping it goes back to the 1950s, when the state commodity inspectors sorted Anxi oolong into three classes for grading: Tieguanyin, se zhong and oolong. The county's other cultivars, more than fifty by one count, were gathered under se zhong.

Four of them are usually named as its core: Ben Shan, Huang Dan, Mao Xie and Mei Zhan. Their histories are patchy. Ben Shan has the clearest record, through a 1937 survey of the Anxi tea trade that puts its discovery about sixty years earlier. Because these teas look and smell close to Tieguanyin, some merchants have sold them under that name, which helps explain why se zhong has so little reputation of its own.
